steps.prompt: What happens to the verb after didn’t and did?
options: It goes back to its base form.
steps.answer: It goes back to its base form.
steps.why: The past is already in did: didn’t think, did it open — not didn’t thought.

steps.title: Past Simple
steps.html:
Regular verbIrregular verb
+He jumped out of the capsule.He fell too fast.
–He didn’t land on his feet.He didn’t think about the view.
?Did he jump at 5.37?Did his parachute open?
short answerYes, he did.No, he didn’t.
was / wereThe team was worried.Eight million people were watching.

Regular verbs add -ed: jump → jumped, land → landed, watch → watched. After -e add only -d: dive → dived.

Irregular verbs change: fall → fell, go → went, take → took, buy → bought, tell → told. There is no rule — learn them.

Negatives and questions use did + the base form for every verb, regular or irregular.

Be is the exception: was / were, with no did: He was safe. Were you frightened?

In the next lesson you will put the Past Simple next to the Past Continuous.

steps.title: Text A — The day I watched a man fall from the sky
steps.html:
I worked for the ground team at Roswell, New Mexico, on 14 October 2012. My job was small — I checked the radios — but I remember every minute.

We waited two weeks for the wind. On an earlier date in October the weather stopped us an hour before launch. Then, on the fourteenth, the desert was still.

At sunrise the balloon went up, enormous, with plastic thinner than a shopping bag. Inside the capsule sat Felix Baumgartner, the Austrian pilot who wanted to jump from the edge of space. The balloon lifted him for two and a half hours, up to almost 39 kilometres.

Then he opened the door and moved forwards onto the step. Nobody spoke. On my screen I saw the curve of the Earth behind him.

He jumped at 5.37 p.m.

For the first half-minute everything looked perfect. He fell towards the desert faster and faster and passed the speed of sound — the first person in history to do that outside an aircraft. Then he started to turn. He went round and round, and we could not stop him. The engineer next to me said nothing. I did not breathe.

Baumgartner pulled out of the spin himself: he pushed his arms backwards and dropped his head. Four minutes and nineteen seconds after he left the capsule, his parachute opened.

He landed on his feet in the desert, and then he fell onto his knees. The rescue team reached him in ninety seconds.

People always ask me the same question: did he know he was in danger? He knew. He climbed into that capsule anyway.

Text A — The day I watched a man fall from the sky

I worked for the ground team at Roswell, New Mexico, on 14 October 2012. My job was small — I checked the radios — but I remember every minute.

We waited two weeks for the wind. On an earlier date in October the weather stopped us an hour before launch. Then, on the fourteenth, the desert was still.

At sunrise the balloon went up, enormous, with plastic thinner than a shopping bag. Inside the capsule sat Felix Baumgartner, the Austrian pilot who wanted to jump from the edge of space. The balloon lifted him for two and a half hours, up to almost 39 kilometres.

Then he opened the door and moved forwards onto the step. Nobody spoke. On my screen I saw the curve of the Earth behind him.

He jumped at 5.37 p.m.

For the first half-minute everything looked perfect. He fell towards the desert faster and faster and passed the speed of sound — the first person in history to do that outside an aircraft. Then he started to turn. He went round and round, and we could not stop him. The engineer next to me said nothing. I did not breathe.

Baumgartner pulled out of the spin himself: he pushed his arms backwards and dropped his head. Four minutes and nineteen seconds after he left the capsule, his parachute opened.

He landed on his feet in the desert, and then he fell onto his knees. The rescue team reached him in ninety seconds.

People always ask me the same question: did he know he was in danger? He knew. He climbed into that capsule anyway.

steps.title: Text B — Two years later, in the same desert
steps.html:
Two years after Baumgartner, a second man went up from the same corner of New Mexico — and almost nobody knew about it.

Alan Eustace was 57, an engineer, and a senior manager at Google. He paid for the project himself. He did not use a capsule at all. He simply hung underneath a helium balloon in a special suit, with a parachute on his back.

On 24 October 2014 the balloon lifted him for two and a half hours, up to 41,419 metres — about two and a half kilometres higher than Baumgartner. Then he cut himself loose. Ninety seconds later he passed the speed of sound. He opened his parachute at about 5,500 metres and landed in the desert fifteen minutes after he left the balloon.

Baumgartner’s team invited the world’s media. Eustace invited one journalist. His altitude record still stands today, and his suit is now in a museum in Washington.

steps.sub: Then choose the correct answer.
steps.prompt: What did Felix Baumgartner become the first person to do?
options: To go faster than the speed of sound.
To fly a balloon into space.
To land in the desert on his feet.
steps.answer: To go faster than the speed of sound.

steps.title: Listen to a radio programme about a second, very different fall.
steps.sub: Then choose the correct answer.
steps.prompt: How did he get up to 38 kilometres?
options: A large balloon lifted him and his capsule.
A plane took him up to the edge of space.
He climbed a mountain and jumped from the top.
steps.answer: A large balloon lifted him and his capsule.

steps.title: Listen to a radio programme about a second, very different fall.
steps.sub: Then choose the correct answer.
steps.prompt: What went wrong immediately after he jumped?
options: He fell too fast and started to turn round and round.
His parachute opened far too early in the fall.
He lost contact with his team on the ground.
steps.answer: He fell too fast and started to turn round and round.

steps.title: Listen to a radio programme about a second, very different fall.
steps.sub: Then choose the correct answer.
steps.prompt: How did his team feel when the parachute opened?
options: They were so pleased he was safe.
steps.answer: They were so pleased he was safe.

steps.title: Write about something that went wrong for you.
steps.sub: Six to eight sentences, in the order it happened. Use the Past Simple.
steps.html:
1. Plan: where you were → what you were doing → what went wrong → what you did → how it ended.
  • Last year / In February …
  • I was …
  • Then …
  • Suddenly …
  • So I …
  • In the end …

• I wrote six or more sentences.
  • The events are in the order they happened.
  • I used at least two irregular past forms.
  • I used one negative with didn’t + base form.

steps.title: Tell the story out loud, then record it.
steps.sub: Tap a line to hear a model first.
items: Last February my brother and I took a lift to the top.
The weather changed, but we didn’t think about it.
Suddenly the snow lifted me up and pulled me down.
My brother called the rescue team.
In the end they pulled me out after eleven minutes.
